examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14062908/assets/ac922b185c42645f703c13d4f5016941b4125d81e85fa5ff529aa5c8d4010ac8.png)

Find the parametric equations of the hyperbola shown above given that its asymptotes are $y=\pm 3x.$
examples.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a vertical hyperbola centered at the origin with Cartesian equation

$$
\dfrac{y^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{x^2}{b^2} = 1
$$

are given by 

$$
x=b\tan{t},\quad y=a\sec{t},
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are positive constants.

The vertices of the hyperbola occur at $(0, \pm a).$ From the graph, we have that $(0,9)$ is a vertex of the hyperbola, so $a=9.$

The asymptotes of a vertical hyperbola are $y = \pm \dfrac{a}{b}x.$ In our case, the asymptotes are $y = \pm 3 x,$ and so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{a}{b} & =3 \\ \frac{9}{b} & =3 \\ b & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the hyperbola are

$$
x=3\tan{t},\quad y=9\sec{t}.
$$

feedback.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a vertical hyperbola centered at the origin with Cartesian equation

$$
\frac{{y}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1
$$

are given by

$$
x=b\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,y=a\operatorname{sec}⁡t.
$$

First, we rewrite the equation of our hyperbola in standard form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}5{y}^{2}-8{x}^{2} & =40 \\ \frac{5{y}^{2}}{40}-\frac{8{x}^{2}}{40} & =\frac{40}{40} \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{8}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{5} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

So, in our case, $a=\sqrt{8}=2\sqrt{2}$ and $b=\sqrt{5}.$ Therefore, the parametric equations are

$$
x=\sqrt{5}\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,y=2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡t.
$$
